In the early 1950s, my father was finishing his theological training in New York, and he always made a point of taking me to the Hudson River piers to see the magnificent ocean liners of that magical era. 

As we barreled south down the elevated West Side Highway in our ‘49 Nash Ambassador, I would position a look-out from the front seat. When spotting 3 orange stacks far ahead, I’d know that the Mary was at dock, or if two stacks, the Elizabeth, or the colors of the handsome Liberte or the Andrea Doria.  

I was 5 years old when the SS United States arrived in the summer of 1952 before her maiden voyage east, and my father made sure that he and I spent an afternoon at the docks in thrilling admiration of that most spectacular vessel.  In this jaded age, it’s hard to describe the innocent pride and profound joy that all of America had in the SS United States.  Yes, there were the noble Cunard Queens of Britain and other fine European liners, but the SSUS was OURS!  It was our ship, America’s ship; the fastest and most modern, and most perfect vision in steel and engineering confidence of the American heart that then knew no boundaries.  

My father is now many years gone, and today, we have lost our flagship to memory; sunk to the deep as yet one more Florida tourist cash cow. There is a sadness in the marrow in knowing that we have also lost that sense of wonder and purpose in the America she once symbolized.  We will never know her or the likes of us again.

It all came about because we were coming back to the US from Germany (Tom was on orders to Vietnam) and had to ship our German Shepherd, too.  We secured the very last kennel for her and came home via "surface" travel. What a "decompress" in between a tour in Germany and his [in] Vietnam. We had 5 glorious days of family time. Our daughter learned to crawl on a big couch in one of the lounges.  We got to spend time with our dog on the kennel deck, which was located on the top deck.  All the animals were treated like royalty by the kennel master. Only drawback of the trip was that we hit a Nor' Easter off Cape Cod.  Passengers and crew alike were told upon arrival in New York that this had been her final voyage.

We cannot reverse the course this administration has set for the country. There will be pain, undoubtedly, and perhaps a great deal of it. Any article about cosmetic surgery should be prefaced with the statement that mental health and social outcomes after cosmetic surgery are entirely unknown as per a recent review article. 

Garbett KM, Paraskeva N, White P, Lewis-Smith H, Smith H, Anquandah J, Diedrichs PC. The psychosocial outcomes following cosmetic surgery are largely unknown: A systematic review. J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg. 2025 May;104:282-297. doi: 10.1016/j.bjps.2025.03.013. Epub 2025 Mar 7. PMID: 40156948.

Surgeons often advertise that self confidence, mood and possibly even earning potential will improve.  However the few longterm ( 10 year) studies that have been done actually show worsened mental health and suicide rates after cosmetic surgery.  Many individuals actually develop depression immediately after surgery.  Some do studies show short term improvements but most are done by the plastic surgery industry so there is a high risk of bias.  There is really no good data to suggest that quality of life improves at all after cosmetic surgery.

I have a special memory, and a tangible souvenir, of Stacy Keach and his Broadway performance as Buffalo Bill.  Growing up in NYC, when balcony seats were $5, my high school friends and I saw everything, usually with the first-run casts.

My friend Mindy Ronner and I sent Stacy Keach a fan letter afterwards about how much we’d enjoyed his performance, but for some reason did this goofy teenage girl thing and wrote it in our high school French.  We must have put a return address on the envelope (our full names and my building) because shortly afterward I received an envelope from Mr. Keach addressed to “Minter\Ronner” and enclosing a card.

The front of the card had a pen-and-colored-ink drawing of Buffalo Bill and his horse, with these word printed below in caps: 

		JE REVIENS (“I will return”).

The hand-written message on the inside of the card said:

	“Dear Rachel & Mindy

		Thank you but I can hardly read French!

		I managed.

					Stacy Keach”

Neither of us had ever received a response from an actor in our young lives, let alone something so personal and customized.  It must have taken thought and effort to find a card with that particular combination of Buffalo Bill and a message in French.  The actual, handwritten thank you note inside was the proverbial cherry on top.

I have kept that note, in its envelope, all these years.  (Don’t want to be too specific about how many, I’ll just say that we were in high school in the late ‘60s).  A wonderful actor and kind man.

I later discovered research showing that an ingredient in broccoli and daikon-radish sprouts (chloforaphane) has been found to reduce the size of tumors in both breast and prostate cancers. It is especially effective in breast-cancer, and also aids chemotherapy and radiation-therapy for those who choose or require those treatments.

I began eating approximately 6-8 ounces per week of the thicker type of broccoli sprouts [not the later-developed and very limp British variation].

 After 6-8 months of my self-therapy, I again had MRI + PMSA-scans, which found that the tumor had receded, and the suspected metastasis to bone had  healed! My tumor was reclassified as Stage-1, with a lower Gleason-score as well. I now have no BPH symptoms, no discomfort, and consider myself healed, as did the oncologist who dismissed me as a patient.

I spent 1 year on a mineral survey project in the Solomon Islands in 1997. Part of that time was in the Short Land Islands where we were only a few kilometers from the PNG border and the southeast end of Bougainville where Yamatoto's plane was shot down. While I knew about the crash site, going there was out of the question as a guerrilla war was underway on the island. Many of the locals I hired to work on the project had family on the PNG side. Through them I learned of many atrocities committed against the Bougainville people by the PNG military and paramilitary force brought in by the government. While the regular PNG military was feared, it was the paramilitary that struck terror in the locals on both sides of the border. Border raids into the Solomon's were enough of a concern that a small government military force was stationed in a nearby village.
I did a fair bit of reading on WW 2 in the Solomon's prior to leaving for the project. From this I learned that the decision to shoot down Yamamoto's plane was taken to the highest level of military and civilian authorities since it was a gray area of accepted war time practice. What sealed Yamamoto's fate was not only the breaking of the Japanese codes, but intelligence information that said Yamamoto operated on a strict time table. This made it possible for US P-38 fighter planes to intercept his aircraft.
I left the Solomon's with a deep sense of respect for the tremendous cost of this war in material and human suffering.

Also I would be curious if any of the older villagers from Mr. Nunu's community have first hand knowledge of the villagers pulling Admiral Yamamoto, if so an oral history would be an invaluable source for historians. The story of Operation Vengence is a story more people should know about as the Pacific Theatre of Operations always gets the short end of the stick in the historiography of World War II. Just a quick note the "Japanese" tank is a Matilda II (A12) Infantry Tank used by the British and Commonwealth forces druing WWII. This vehicle was likely part of the ANZAC (Australian and New Zealand Army Corp) operations in 1944 or 1945 to oust the Japanese from the island. The Matilda II was considered obsolete in the European Theatre of Operations by 1943 due to rapid advances in tank development in the theatre but soldiered on in the Pacific with ANZAC troops until the final days of WWII. Pardon my nitpicking but I am a historian and I couldn't resist!

Eventually technology will also make it clear that we don’t have free will, at least not in the sense of how we normally think of free will. Right now, we feel that we are in control of what we do and think, but once machines are able to predict our every move and thought, we’ll be confronted by the disturbing truth that this is all just an illusion.

And if that isn’t disturbing enough, technology will then show that there isn’t even any ‘I’ in the first place. That is, we believe that there is an ‘I’: something that makes me me, and gives me my true identity that differentiates me from anyone else. But once technology gains the power to manipulate our bodies, brains, and minds at will, we’ll quickly realize that also this notion of the ‘I’ is an illusion: a nice way to parse and make sense of the world but that can be brought to a breaking point by technology.

In sum, some technologies really should not be pursued, as they can shatter our sense of who or what we are.

comments.name: Jazzie

Our father had preceded us there the year before, on a former troop ship, the Arosa Star, in order to establish himself. We  sailed across the Atlantic for 5 days through turbulent weather. My mother was seasick for the duration; we kids had a grand time exploring the ship. There was a children’s playroom with panoramic windows at the stern; my strongest memory is coming up the St. Lawrence River, seeing garbage being discarded into the river and thinking, “That’s not right!”. We landed in Montreal and ate at a café that had ‘chien chaud’ (hot dogs) on the menu, which my mother translated – it sounded disgusting! We then boarded a train for the trip to Calgary – no berths, just seats. We were among the cohort of 282,200 immigrants to Canada that year, the highest single-year total recorded since 1913 at the time; photographer took a photo of my little brother and sister which made the papers.

My one experience with this ship:
     On the day of the return of the "United States" from Europe on its July 1952 maiden voyage, a school friend and I had taken a rowboat out from Brooklyn for some fishing. We knew nothing about the boat's impending return.Not paying attention, we had been swept by the current to somewhere in the middle of the Narrows. Looking up, we saw a huge ship heading directly at us blowing its horn. I stood up and shrugged showing our helpless situation which forced the ship  to tack left to avoid a direct hit. As the ship (much too closely) passed us, I saw "United States" written on its bow and watched in awe as it went by, its wake almost capsizing our boat. Unaware of our dangerous situation celebrating passengers  were on deck smiling and waving at us! We had to hitch a ride on a fishing vessel to get back.I wonder if the ship's log notated this incident

comments.name: David

I sailed on the SS United States in the spring of 1957. I was almost 10. We were moving to England for 9 months (ended up being 6 years).  I travelled with my older brother and mother.  My father flew.  My mother would not fly so that’s why we sailed; New York to Southampton.  I became a part of a group of young kids. We were in cabin class but knew how to get into 1st class. We used to play elevator tag.  Taking the elevators up or down to avoid being it.  Sometimes we would cheat and take the stairs. I remember the dinner chimes and playing shuffleboard. In the evening we would play horse races in the lounge and I would win some money occasionally.  I would watch movies in the theater.  I did not like the swimming pool; it was salt water and would slosh around as the ship would pitch and roll. 

After landing in Southampton, I took a day or so to stop thinking I was on board ship.  I was used to the pitching and rolling.  I thought it was a very noisy ship.  While in England we returned to the US on other ships, a total of 4 trans Atlantic crossings.

comments.name: A geologist

Geologists are raconteurs of the past using the tools of science, technology, fact based problem solving. More and more we are at a great loss because our expertise shouts things to us that are mostly being ignored, for the scoop and what sells well in press. NYT has been one of the welcome few main stream exceptions.

More and more we see increasingly threatened and endangered species, as well as extinctions. These glaringly look like we're at the beginning of a mass extinction event—how bad will it develop is anyone's guess. A problem is despite the obvious trends there are no good baselines or species numbers for comparisons; that would take coursing many professions, ornithologists, biologists, wildlife biologists, zoologists, ecologists, entamologsts, ichthyologists, herpetologists, on and on. Which is not being done in a broad reaching or comprehensive manner.

That said, we are wondering and many are petrified—no pun intended—what will it take for the realities to sink in before it's too late?

Excessive heat is tapping us on the shoulder, roaming spring to fall heat domes and overheated oceans. Waters off CA are now 14° above normal leading to mass die offs.

Many expect things to "return to normal." We are well beyond normals, having triggered ever more complex feedbacks that guarantee change, the kind of change that can and will swallow us... unless. That is my language, understood by one who has carefully studied bones for years, for those listening.

comments.body: I'm going to thank doomscrolling for bringing about brain stacking. My grandmother's mental picture of a pendulum swinging and applying to everything, is stuck in my head. A choice automatically starts the swing back in the opposite direction. The brain stack has helped me and I'm in my late 60s. Not set in my ways, no sireee.

comments.name: SteveWr.
comments.body:
I had been doom scrolling for the previous 10+ years, coinciding with my first smartphone. I am a news junkie, and would be the first to admit that it's very addicting, especially because I have wide interests and use several news aggregators. It may keep my cognition from deteriorating, but it's exhausting, depressing, and the negative content precludes sharing with others in a social setting. 

I finally broke my habit when I discovered, by chance, that I had an unknown talent for driftwood sculpture. My creations are not everyone's cup of tea, but the creativity they have engendered make me happy, motivated, and ravenous for other creative outlets. 

I've discovered that phone time has receeded in importance as the constant input of digital facts and news definitely numbed and dulled my brain. I now feel sorry for those who don't have any hobbies, and are struggling to find meaning in a superficial digital wasteland.

comments.name: MmeDeFarge
comments.body: Otherwise known as "doing stuff" and "messing around." Good for the Zs! Ironic, though, that they're adopting a term ("stacking") that comes from computer programming, to which this activity is meant to offer an antidote. Language matters. Gen Zs, time to stop optimizing, maxxing and stacking and just start messing around.

articles.title: Doomscrolling? Try Brain Stacking.
articles.summary: A trend promises the antidote to burnout and brain rot. There is some science to back it up.

comments.name: Linda
comments.body:
I am tried of all of this, when can we return to a nation that supports its citizens and follows the rule of law.  
Maybe we could do better as citizens and elect honorable people.
No one should be above the law and the law should not favor the money class.
Please let MAGA finally die.

comments.name: Not An Aikenite
comments.body:
It’s most interesting that Blanche said that Miller has a lawyer and it’s Blanche! I thought Blanche said he was Trump’s lawyer. So who does Blanche represent?
Personally I think Blanche should be impeached and then disbarred.

comments.name: CDW
comments.body: Is the Will Scharf mentioned in this article the same Will Scharf who has stood behind Trump for a couple of years like a mindless automaton handing Trump those Ruth Cris style menu boards for him to sign???

comments.name: Jon Asher
comments.body: Donald Trump's efforts to weaponize the DOJ have, up until election day, been largely successful.  By that I don't mean they've won important cases, because it appears as if they haven't won any.  What I mean is that Trump, Blanche and the other White House toadies have managed to specifically target Trump's enemies, causing them serious problems as they fight back.  BUT, at the same the the long list of those who have either been forced out or resigned is a solid indication of how structurally weak the DOJ has become.  This is the result of vindictive policies that fly in the face of what the American people want, something that was said loud and clear on November 3.  If Trump, Miller, Blanche and the others continue to pursue their course of action the result will be an even bigger repudiation of the Republican party in 2028.  My guess is that such a humiliation/repudiation will spell the end of the Republican party as a major factor in American politics.  The disconnect between senior Republican officials and the voters who might support them is widening by the day.  Let's hope the Republicans decide to run JD Vance in '28.  I can't wait!

comments.name: Susan in CT
comments.body: The Hegseth vote was a disaster - but one that we can plan for in two year. However that time, which should be brought up immediately Democrats in Congress must be sure to push stronger language that would block the Secretary from being appointed to the Senate in Tennessee. The newly elected governor there is waiting to appoint Hegseth into her old seat in the Senate. Marsha Blackburn has not been secretive about her plans to give a life line into Congress. Wording into a vote should be a final say into any further job in the federal government.

comments.name: chris
comments.body: And the US is supposed to have the most fair justice system in the world?

comments.name: KW
comments.body: Blanche has agreed to turn the Department of Justice into Trump's own attack dog law firm.  While DOJ is wasting its time and taxpayer money pursuing Tramp's personal vendettas, who is going after sex traffickers, drug cartels, criminals who defraud Americans of their savings, etc.?  This is not what America wants.  Trump is fueling the Blue Wave of 2028.

comments.name: MP
comments.body:
The articles talks about all of the DOJ court losses, but even in those cases Trump wins. He has imposed costs on these private litigants in the tens of thousands of dollars and in some cases in the hundreds of thousands of dollars. (I wonder what James Comey's legal fees are?)

How many people are willing to make a statement or take an action knowing that it will cost them $40 - 100K even though they will ultimately "win".  Trump is a master of legal tactics. Prior to his presidency, he filed and had filed against him hundreds of legal cases. Trump wants to be in court and knows how to use the courts to his advantage.

What Congress should do is to pass a bill, that would automatically pay the legal fees and all expenses of parties that the DOJ sues or indicts for their past public service, if their case is dismissed or they win. This should include cases where the US settles with the defendant. 

The taxpayer is paying for the DOJ to weaponize their attorneys, the private individuals should be made whole. Payments would be made immediately and automatically, even if the government appeals. Otherwise, the DOJ successfully penalizes, the people who stand up to Trump, even when these people win their cases.

articles.title: A Diminished Justice Dept. Braces for Fresh Fights After Midterm Loss
articles.summary: The upheaval points to a broader dilemma spurred by the election: whether the department can carry out President Trump’s priorities as career officials eye the exits and senior department officials resign.

comments.name: Anon
comments.body:
More math I don’t understand. Ms. Chen makes $58,000 a year and is married to an employed person. Her work pays for health insurance and she and her husband pay only $12,000 a year in rent and utilities. Including her husband’s pay, that seems to be quite a bit of money with which to raise children. 

I’m not saying that child care providers should not be sufficiently well paid, but many of us made significant financial and life sacrifices to raise our children. Hers and her husband’s is living with parents.

comments.name: Otis
comments.body:
This just shows that someone has to pay for “free” government services. In this case it’s taxpayers and an army of low paid childcare providers. 

And just because a government service is “free” it does not mean it’s of high quality. It seems to me many of these workers are underpaid, stressed and overworked. This likely won’t result in the children getting the attention they need.

comments.name: Long-time User
comments.body: I wonder if volunteers could supplement this workforce. Retirees (or younger people of means) who don't (or do!) have their own grandchildren but enjoy little kids and have some free time and are willing to get the training/screening? Is that crazy?

comments.name: Nina
comments.body: This article is so good, and the photos tell so much. Human progress means taking care of each other, the hardest work, with long consequences. Little ones who are properly seen, heard, fed, and tended to cost the government far less as they grow up than kids who are neglected cost us. Your deep reporting on the cost of fulfilling Mamdani's campaign promise is invaluable and I hope will be carefully studied by early childhood scholars   in the coming decades. What is more important? Nina Butts

comments.name: Rosalind Renouard
comments.body: When children 0 to 5 are exposed to appropriate early learning and childcare, everyone benefits. The creation of a strong early learning environment creates a win, win situation for all.  Head Start should continue to serve those who can't afford childcare and early learning, and those who benefit which are all of us - parents, community, business, county, local government - should do our share.  Mamdani is on the right path.  If children go to school ready to learn, high school graduation rates improve, crime decreases and the business community benefits by having an educated workforce. And, the country benefits from all of the above.

comments.name: MM
comments.body: Honestly? Forget CEOs. Childcare providers are one-of-a-kind. The level of patience and empathy they can summon for ten plus kids that are not even their own is superhuman. They are juggling complex, dynamic tasks all the time, simultaneously managing the development for all these different kids who are all at different stages, with different personalities and needs -- and the stakes (our literal future as a society) could not be higher. $33k? In NYC? They should be making at least $100k.

comments.name: Sparky
comments.body:
Yes, these women are underpaid and that needs to be addressed. 

But the NYC budget is currently $127B, the highest in the world, and Mamdani wants to add tens of billions to it. NYC residents already pay the highest combined income taxes in the United States on top of substantial property and sales taxes.

If Mamdani can get the money from taxing people who make over $1,000,000 a year, great. But a few months ago he threatened to spike property taxes on 3,000,000 NYC homeowners most of whom make far less than 7 figures annually. I hope he has learned his lesson.

comments.name: Joanne
comments.body: Thank you for this important article. The issues you raise face child care providers throughout California. I've been a child care policy consultant for over 25 years. Every single study I do shows a shortage of spaces, low wages, averaging 50% of public school teachers, and providers face maintenance and repairs that never have enough funding. Providers want to expand but don't have extra profit to fund debt service. Many middle income families make too much to quality for subsidies but spend 20 to 30% of income on child care. Making Family Home Child Care legal as of a right, without permits in California has helped increase supply. State grants for maintenance and repairs and new construction has also been beneficial. There are multiple studies in the US showing the economic benefits of early care and education yet our federal government is trying to dismantle Head Start.

articles.title: The Workers on the Front Lines of Mamdani’s Free Child Care Plan
articles.byline: Emma G. Fitzsimmons and Anna Connors
articles.summary: The mayor’s plan for universal child care relies on tens of thousands of workers who are among New York City’s lowest paid. He pledged to raise their pay, but doing so requires more state funding.

comments.name: AKJersey
comments.body:
The Democratic landslide was due to only one issue.
The price of gas is high, and Trump is blamed.
Other issues and particulars of Democratic and Republican candidates were largely irrelevant.
The Democratic Congress has a mandate to lower fuel costs, and maybe the cost of hamburger.
If that isn't done, the Democrats will lose in 2028.

comments.name: SFNative
comments.body: Of the 40 House seats that Democrats flipped, 38 were won by moderates and only 2 by extremist "progressives".  The one non-gerrymandered House seat flipped by Republicans (in northern Maine) was lost because a progressive nominee replaced a moderate incumbent.  Of the 8 Senate seats flipped by Democrats, 7 were won by moderates and only one (ME), which would not have been challenging with a moderate candidate, was won by a progressive.  The two already-blue Senate seats that were endangered needlessly (MI and MN) were risked by nominating progressives.

comments.name: Terry Mulcaire
comments.body:
Economic inequality has been getting worse for nearly fifty year in this country.  The percentage of wealth owned by the very richest few has increased many-fold since then, and the share owned by the rest of us has shrunk correspondingly.  Last week's election showed that lots of people are finally seeing this, and that they--we--are very very unhappy about it.

Calling efforts to reverse this trend "economic populism" risks making it sound radical.  What we really need to do is reverse this disastrous trend, and start heading back to something like normalcy, to a division of wealth that, unlike our current, is consistent constitutional democracy.  It's really not radical in the least.

comments.name: PeterJ
comments.body:
Whenever I read about "economic populism" i'm missing the writers clarification of what he/she understands as populism. Populism suggests a simplistic, mostly misleading concept intended to gain support with less sophisticated audience. But there is nothing misleading in what most Democratic politicians argue for while they comprise necessary policies to maintain a well-to-do society, one that we can expect the richest country to afford. The most important elements of such enjoy broad support across Americans as well a broad support with economists. For instance,
1. A more just tax system that shrinks the enormous wealth gap between the richest and the rest of (99%) of Americans. The proceeds of a reformed tax policy should support long-term viability of Social Security and should bring financial viability for universal healthcare and alleviate the financial burdens  of education and home ownership.
2. Big money should be eliminated from politics, especially from elections
3. Reform of the Supreme Court that has degenerate over recent decades by bif money and corporate interests.
4. Strict crackdown of government corruption.

I don't see anything in these goals that doesn't align with the majority opinions of not just that of the American society but also with those economic, juristic, scientific scholars'. So why to call it populism?

comments.name: Elliot
comments.body: Can we rely on the corrupt to fight corruption? Schumer et al stand in the way of a winning agenda because they EMBODY the corruption that voters want to cleanse.

comments.name: Charles Ferldt
comments.body: It's really, it's just the folks trying to create fractures that are.

comments.name: Antidisestablishment Dem
comments.body:
Economic populism will never work.  What we have done is that we have over promised on Universal Healthcare, Universal Basic Income, Universal Childcare, Free Tuition, Rent/Home subsidies, etc.  To anyone with a calculator these are things that we cannot afford.  We are already in debt to the tune of $40 trillion and the debt service costs (interest payments) are already threatening national priorities.  Even if we could continue to live off the credit card, we would need to provide incentives for investors to buy Treasury Bonds by raising interest rates.  

As a financial expert, I would point out that we need to roll back the Bush/Trump tax cuts, hire auditors at the IRS to collect the $700 billion plus revenues that we are owed, but are not being paid.  We need to address Social Security or else we will have even more elderly people living out of their cars in 2032.  

But what have we done?  We made a bunch of promises that we cannot keep.

comments.name: Insight
comments.body:
It's not complicated.  What the US media refers to as "Economic Populism" is what the rest of the civilized world considers to be the political center, and therefore has broad support within the Democratic party as well as a majority of the voters in this country.  "Democratic Socialism", the idea that the middle class should not be utterly and completely at the mercy of the wealthy, is what the rest of the world considers center-left.  
However, the lack of anything "radical" associated with these policy outlooks doesn't drive clicks and views like a good fight, so the media looks to fabricate evidence for conflict wherever it can.

articles.title: For Democrats, Economic Populism Is Cutting Through Party Divides
articles.summary: Moderate Democrats and progressives have long feuded over who should drive their party’s economic agenda. But many newly elected members say they share the same big goals.

comments.name: Charlie
comments.body: The article “How much does being able to drive matter to you?” By Shannon Dwayne, Widens my perspective overall of those different from me and communities different from mine. I know for a fact my eyes light up at the idea of me behind a wheel, and my friends the same. Driving for the first time hands a freedom that has never been handed too one before. But it also comes with a Level of maturity that not all teens of driving age have acquired. Being behind the wheel needs maturity for the pure fact that it is deadly, If one is not mature behind the wheel and making right decisions, they may die. Many teens aren’t ready to drive, and some parents aren’t ready to hand the keys to the younger generation.

comments.name: Beckett Down
comments.body: As someone that is about to get their permit, and eventually license, driving means a lot to me. It is the start of being able to drive wherever you want and gain freedom. But, it also comes with a lot of responsibility too. This could be one of the reasons why less and less teenagers are getting their license. They may not have a trusted person to drive with when they are nervous, or don’t want to get into an accident because of that weight on their shoulders that new drivers have. We also have to compare the past circumstances with today's and realize that evolution is a thing. In the past we only had a bike or scooter to our access before being able to drive. So naturally a car would feel like much more of a treasure and valuable. However, with the new era of electric vehicles— e-bikes, e-scooters and e-motos — brings less of a desire and need for a teenager to get a license and drive because you can go just as fast. Even in a time where all of these factors are relevant, driving still matters to me.

comments.name: Katerina
comments.body: I would say that getting my driver’s license definitely matters to me. It’s a right of passage for teenagers because it gives us independence and freedom. A lot of teenagers now are probably used to having their parents drive them around to anywhere they wanna go. In other words they don’t feel the need to get their license because they don’t see the reason to. There are also other modes of transportation—busses, trains, bikes—which can make getting a license less appealing. I currently have my permit and I can’t wait to get my actual license and to fully have that freedom of being to go anywhere at any time.

comments.name: Mario
comments.body: Learning to drive in the long run is a priority of mine. I believe that current day teens don’t have it as an utmost priority due to the ease of talking to friends online. In other words, due to the easy accessibility of communication in the modern age, especially being a standard with teens. Driving is important and I doubt many teens plan to never get their license, but I don’t think they are flocking to the DMV like years past. People don’t need to be driven as much anymore—now anyone can be with anyone at any point. Still people want to actually be with each other, although it's not a need in hanging out.

comments.name: Lily
comments.body: I think that our generation has began to steer away from viewing driving as a privilege. Since there are so many other ways to get around like Uber, public transportation, or even E-Bikes, learning to drive might not always be as common anymore - some people don’t even ever learn how to drive because they don’t feel the need to. In other words, driving used to be the primary way to get from place to place. But, since there are so many other options available, it is sometimes looked over even though it is an important skill to learn.

comments.name: Lily
comments.body: Only about 57 percent of teenagers get their driver’s license by the end of high school. I hope to achieve my license as soon as I can. It has always been very important for me to eventually be able to drive because I’ve simply just always wanted to drive myself around. More people my age put it off because it’s lots of work and time. When I think about driving, I feel excited to gain freedom in where and when I can go places. I am a bit nervous for the tests and classes. Overall, I think people should get their license as soon as possible.

comments.name: Jorge Jimenez
comments.body: I think being able to drive is important for teenagers because it gives them freedom and independence. Some teenagers are not in a rush to get their license because they are used to having their parents drive them everywhere or getting rides from friends. The article says only about 57 percent of teenagers get their license by the end of high school, compared to more than 80 percent in the 1980s and 1990s. Technology is one reason because nowadays we can do everything online, including shopping, entertainment, and talking to friends. Personally, I am still working on getting my permit, and I look forward to getting my license. I want to go places without depending on my parents for a ride. Driving is a big part of growing up because it teaches responsibility and helps you become independent. At the same time, I understand why teenagers might feel nervous because driving is a responsibility and you have to pay attention to everything around you. I think my generation is less in a hurry to grow up because we have more ways to entertain ourselves at home. In the past, teenagers had to go outside or drive somewhere to meet friends, but now people can text, call, or play games online. I think parents are more protective because they worry about their kids' safety. Overall, I think getting a driver's license is an important milestone. Even if teenagers are not rushing to get one, having the ability to drive can make life easier and give them more choices.

comments.name: Addy M
comments.body: For me, getting my drivers license is a big deal. Not only is it a big responsibility that my parents are entrusting me with - - a good responsibility - - but I will have a new sense of freedom that I have never had before. Though I will have to put in some effort to accomplish this task, I think that it will be very much worth it. But, I believe that many kids around my age feel the opposite way. I don’t understand why many kids nowadays don’t want to get their license. I have many friends with their license, and they say it was very much worth it. Regardless, being able to drive really matters  to me.

articles.title: How Much Does Being Able to Drive Matter to You?
articles.summary: Why do you think fewer teenagers today are rushing to get their driver’s license?

comments.name: True Blue
comments.body: So much sorrow. The firefighters are incredible and to have to deal with loss time and time again is beyond painful.

comments.name: Trudy
comments.body: There is a lot of construction in NYC without this sort of thing happening.  Corners were obviously cut - it would not surprise me to see criminal liability for someone down the line here.  City codes should mimic London's - they have a whole regime for this sort of excavation and they don't seem to have these issues.

comments.name: Karen
comments.body: This exact tragedy happened in Philadelphia in 2013. A building  next to a Salvation Army was being demoed by a builder who cut corners and it collapsed. Seven people died senselessly and others were left with life altering injuries.  Older buildings in cities need to be rebuilt, but somebody has to be watching that the surrounding buildings  are safe and secure. I’m guessing the Brooklyn builder had paid a fortune in permits which means the city is supposed to be on top of these things.

comments.name: Janet Keefer.
comments.body: I watch many of the home rehab shows of The Property Brothers, Drew and Jonathan Scott. The ALWAYS carefully check a building’s foundation before any work starts. I am amazed at the slipshod construction of many houses, such as sistered support beams that merely rest on two-by-fours or just dirt, and inadequate roof and upper-story support beams. I would have thought the inspection process for major construction would be strict across the board but especially in neighborhoods where new construction abuts construction that might have been done two centuries ago. Scary.

comments.name: Nan
comments.body: This is not the first time this sort of event has happened in Brooklyn; I recall a collapse a few years back. Pretty much the same scenario, with the collapsed structure also an old residential building. Something is missing in survey/regulation/inspection system. In a city with so many very old buildings, this must be a really rigorous process. Tragedies will continue if the city does not address this.

comments.name: Lifestyler
comments.body: Friends of mine rented a flat in Paris, France, next to a building that was demolished and became an excavation site. Their building showed cracks after a few weeks of work. They got out as fast as they could.

comments.name: AS
comments.body: While I applaud the push for more housing in NYC, I'm extremely concerned about the fact that it's being speeded up, possibly without enough consideration for safety, including not enough inspectors. This includes new buildings as well as renovations (recall the office-to-residential conversion in Manhattan that resulted in buckling columns). Why do we let such essentials as housing (not enough) come to a point of desperation, and then rush in what is almost a panic to solve it? (Rhetorical question)

comments.name: L
comments.body: Survey monitoring of adjacent properties should be a requirement. It’s likely this building was moving slightly for weeks before the collapse…digging too quickly and undermining a foundation can lead to subsidence of a foundation and tragedy:(

articles.title: Excavation Was Taking Place Next to Building in Brooklyn That Collapsed
articles.summary: New York City officials had ordered work at the construction site to stop after an apartment building in the Flatbush neighborhood collapsed onto it.

comments.name: Meg
comments.body:
Thank you for the  picture of the Maplewood train station.
Never had to commute from there,but had my first driving lesson to park at the station.
Definitely it was a tight fit.
Hello and thank you to all the brave and hardy NJ commuters.
Best wishes from rural NH with no public transit.

comments.name: Bill
comments.body:
The commutes are, at best, unpredictable.  The Midtown Direct service has been cut back, and as noted is subject to all of the vagaries of the bridge construction.  Ditto trying to drive to Newark unless you are taking the PATH, which has also been overcrowded.  Driving to Secaucus is expensive but you tend to have more options, even now.  

I've given up driving to the city -- it's just irritating paying the tolls/commuter surcharge and realizing NJ is not receiving any benefit from it.

Working from home even part of the week makes this bearable.

comments.name: Anon
comments.body: This is more of a case for allowing more work from home where and when possible. So much time wasted on a commute that I'm sure does not help make people more productive.

comments.name: Jacqueline
comments.body: I’m fortunate to do a reverse-commute via car that doesn’t take more than 20 min at the worst. I’m curious: how many hours per week are people actually working when they have these long commutes?

comments.name: Robin
comments.body:
None of the 4 provide a true picture of the commute. My husband commuted for 35 years  on NJTransit to Penn Station, which, until the recent changes because of repairs, Portal Bridge, etc that eliminates Midtown Direct for a timeperiod, allowed him to leave the house get to the train station and be in Penn Station within 45 minutes. He and many of our neighbors routinely took the 7:10 from the Orange NJ station. Return trip in the evening was and still is  a totally different story.
An analysis requires a week or 2-week period to determine what is and is not an outlier. For example, timing the commute on Election Day when  traffic is less and passengers are fewer than on other days doesn't give a true picture of the daily commute. Additionally given my husband's and most of our neighbors's commuting schedules, even leaving the house at 7:15 is relatively late. NJTranist at South ORange, Orange and East Orange are most crowded for the 7am-7:30 trains. 
Finally - the return trip. NJTransit schedules are are closer to every half hour - 45 minutes after 5:30. WHich means those leaving the office even at 5 risk missing the trains that are scheduled every 10-15 minutes.

comments.name: Cookie
comments.body: These are great!  Thank you for taking us along on your commute.  Makes my garage to garage 20 minute commute, while listening to a book, feel indolent.  Stephen's was my favorite, Ronda's second.

comments.name: Bruce Goodrich
comments.body: Quite some years back I worked for a producer, for a year, whose offices were at 72nd and Broadway.  I commuted from Montclair, which involved about a three-block walk from my apartment, to the bus stop, then the bus route through Upper Montclair to the Lincoln Tunnel, to Port Authority.  Then, the 1, 2 or 3, Subway up to 72nd (the express, if the timing was right).  If all was running smoothly (no tunnel jam or subway delay), it took about an hour, an hour and ten, door-to-door.  Montclair is lovely and leafy, and I always felt I was leaving ‘the country’ to go to Manhattan.

comments.name: Zamboanga
comments.body: My commute consisted of getting out of bed, walking down three flights of stairs, having breakfast and then down a few stairs (ladders) to the engine room of a container ship. That was the good part.

articles.title: How 4 Seasoned Commuters Make It From New Jersey to Manhattan
articles.byline: Stefanos Chen, Patrick McGeehan, Stephen Merelman, Tracey Tully and Ronda Kaysen
articles.summary: Crossing the Hudson River on a weekday this fall has required planning, patience and, sometimes, luck. Four New York Times employees put their routes to the test.

comments.name: Annie Blue
comments.body: Trump appears to be having cognitive/neurological issues.  Many think he has frontotemporal dementia.   That is aside from his malevolent, masochistic narcissism many suggest.

comments.name: D
comments.body: In the next year or two I fully expect Trump to stagger, stumble, and ultimately pratfall, splayed and blubbering, in full-blown incoherence of the sort which is indecipherable even to the most trusted Trump-speak interpreters. The wheels in his head are winding down, the spokes worn, the gears slipping, the old belts and pulleys frayed and snapping audibly with every misanthropic murmuration of his misbegotten mind.

comments.name: Thomas Mac
comments.body: Trump is not a smart person. He normally speaks at a 5th-grade level (equal to a 10 year old). He is not well read, he never prepares and he eschews details because, frankly, all of that is beyond his intellect. So he often just makes stuff up in a sad effort to sound more intelligent and informed than he ever really is. And now, on top of all this, he is experiencing the normal cognitive hiccups that come with being 80 years old. When you think about it, this is a big part of why he is such a terrible president. Smart, well-spoken and smart-minded people usually don’t fail this spectacularly.

comments.name: Sam J
comments.body: While he is definitely making some weird sounds and is almost certainly unwell... As someone who worked around teleprompters for years, the shipyardCREE one seems like a very obvious teleprompter reading error- and he has a lot of these.  He will read ahead and then realize he was meant to stop at a certain point and missed his pause, or/and he often seems to double-back to add some (usually as equally confusing) ad-lib.

comments.name: Jenny Justice
comments.body: I have watched video of these speech oddities and been amazed at people's capacity to ignore the obvious. These are clearly involuntary exclamations - something is very wrong with the man who has put our entire country at war.

comments.name: Elbows
comments.body:
I’m a speech language pathologist and all of us demonstrate verbal revisions and semantic errors. 

The issue is that Trump demonstrates a tangential thought process in which he jumps from subject to subject. Add in those revisions and it borders on nonsensical.

articles.title: What Are Those Strange Noises Trump Makes?
articles.summary: These are erratic executive eruptions.

comments.name: David
comments.body:
It's a question of goals:

In the past, the goal was for America to be successful, regardless of who led it. The losing candidate would naturally think their approach was better, but would still hope for good outcomes regardless

Now, it's all about winning. If the candidate loses, then there's nothing else to be gained. They hope the winner goes on to lose, and for America to lose so they can say, "told you so" and maybe come to power the next time

comments.name: Ceci56
comments.body: I think less that it’s no longer a “given” than politics have become so blatantly dirty, uncivil, and corrupt. The end result is we have more players who are of lesser character. What Ramaswamy did to Acton was abhorrent, that void of civility set up her having to create a firm boundary, and the message was clear. This unwillingness to apologize, and then double down, is where the real problem lies.

comments.name: Christine
comments.body: Mike Roger's was too busy calling PATIENTS he sued asking if they would "settle" for a lower amount.

comments.name: Jim
comments.body:

comments.name: A geologist
comments.body:
Geologists are raconteurs of the past using the tools of science, technology, fact based problem solving. More and more we are at a great loss because our expertise shouts things to us that are mostly being ignored, for the scoop and what sells well in press. NYT has been one of the welcome few main stream exceptions.

More and more we see increasingly threatened and endangered species, as well as extinctions. These glaringly look like we're at the beginning of a mass extinction event—how bad will it develop is anyone's guess. A problem is despite the obvious trends there are no good baselines or species numbers for comparisons; that would take coursing many professions, ornithologists, biologists, wildlife biologists, zoologists, ecologists, entamologsts, ichthyologists, herpetologists, on and on. Which is not being done in a broad reaching or comprehensive manner.

That said, we are wondering and many are petrified—no pun intended—what will it take for the realities to sink in before it's too late?

Excessive heat is tapping us on the shoulder, roaming spring to fall heat domes, overheated oceans, extreme weather intensification. En Nino waters off CA are 14° above normal leading to mass die offs.

Many expect a "return to normal." We are beyond normals, having triggered complex feedbacks that guarantee change, the kind of change that can and will swallow us... unless. That is my language, understood by one who has carefully studied bones for years, for those listening.

It would be great if articles that contain (or *should* contain) important info/data/metrics that can be quantified do so. At the very least, they should make more of an effort to clarify the direction, range, etc., or say why the information can't be any more precise. 

For example: "Once an A.I. model becomes proficient in the sandbox, as measured by false positives and false negatives ..." 

That sounds like there is some metric but does not say what it is (it doesn't even say "reduced" to indicate the direction of the measurement) and also doesn't indicate that the metric is classified, or give another reason for not providing more clarity. 

Then two paragraphs later there's a reference to a single person's observation of the system's performance: "statistics from training showed false positives of less than 5 percent". It also says that there's a "secrecy agreement with Avenger Labs." 

But this later reference doesn't connect any of the earlier dots: is this 5% observation more or less than the proficiency goal alluded to above? Or is the reference to a secrecy agreement here why there was no metric earlier? And if it is secret, is to try to deflect any accusation of unacceptable collateral damage that accompanies false positives?  

The operational and moral considerations may not have clear answers but there's no excuse not to make the simple things clear.

Well, the collection here is somewhat better than so many of the identity obsessed pieces of work which seems these days to be mostly narcisstic self images of POC's. How boring and unremarkable (let's not call it trash culture of guilt obsessed curators). Just a few years back that kind of work wouldn't be accepted: now not so. One step above, dare I say it? 'Paint By Color kits'. So IMHO art cannot be distinguished by ethnicity. Does anyone care that Picasso was Spanish? (& not French even though he spent so much time in Montmartre).  Or that Franz Kline was a German American? (I believe). Certainly not that Warhola was the origin of Warhol. This rise of black artists via their identity is again IMHO our cultural decline via societal guilt which wouldn't be so bad if it were any good. How many times have I stood in front of Guernica, mesmerized or in front of a Matisse – based on its power. (certainly Gaugin which could be considered the early manifestation of ethnic subjects – w/its brown skinned, heavy limbed beauties.) You hadda be there he claimed.  Another manifestation of misguided policy. Read Spengler's Decline of the West.

Judging by the works in the accompanying photographs, I would say it is long overdue.  But the identity part does trouble me.  Was it just black abstract artists who were ignored by the critics and the mainstream contemporary art market?  Or were there other avant garde abstract artists - white, Hispanic, Asian, outsider artists of whatever ethnicity, & etc. - who also failed to gain critical acclaim for whatever reason and whose work still holds up today?  Honestly, there would have to be.  And we may never see their work.  This is an important exhibition which I support and wish every success. But because it confines itself to only one identity, I think it's only telling part of a much larger story.

comments.name: Risk
comments.body:
Nvidia does not meet Philip Fisher’s qualitative standards on points 15 (integrity), 14 (open communication during trouble), 9 (depth of management), and 8 (executive relations and board oversight). A “one-man” Jensen Huang show will not resolve the organization’s current troubles. U.S. export laws were potentially circumvented throughout 2024 and 2025, with federal investigators probing whether some of the $4.8 billion in chips were transferred into China via Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia.
China is restricting purchases of Nvidia products, and Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta are developing their own custom chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia.
Nvidia’s off-balance-sheet vendor financing by issuing tens of billions in lease and credit guarantees—along with its AI equity acquisitions jumping from $7 billion to $99 billion over the last 12 months to tie non-profitable AI companies to its products—further increases circular financing risks.
Add to it the global push-back against data centers that are potentially under-utilized with technology changing constantly, a perfect storm.
An organization with an outstanding, competitive product line does not need to resort to these very risky tactics of buying into its non-profitable customers in order to sell them its equipment.
The November 17 earnings call will be all fluff. Make no mistake: this company carries substantial risks, and investors should stay away.

comments.name: Expat who votes
comments.body:
What I read about these data centers ruining neighborhoods and pristine nature areas terrifies me. And yet we are clearly already in a dog-eating-its-tail reality. We are using AI everywhere. 

Curious to put AI to the test (ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude) I attempted some short cuts in preparing teaching materials; this after a series of workshops for educators last year extolling the virtues of AI in education. The few times I have tried have been at times wonderful, but usually with glitches that underscore how important it is that AI be treated as a tool. 

I last used each of the three over the summer, with a non-paying account. This week I returned for help with a new activity, and each one of the three cut off my use after only 2-3 queries unless I used a paid upgrade, making me wait 6-8 hours for my next free session time. 

So I guess we can say the tech behemoths are counting on the masses to pay for the data centers. 

I’d love to return to life in the early 1990’s. No cell phones, no internet, few pcs.

comments.name: Ore Williams
comments.body: I do not follow any health or wellness influencers—anyone can come on the internet and say they are a “health guru” or  a doctor, but that doesn’t mean they are. Not having any credible information to back up their claims, especially in the age of A.I, makes it even harder to tell who’s credible or not. Watching the video, I learned that there are people and companies around the world (specifically the US and China) to sell supplements, toys, etc. As a teenager, it can be easier to tell the difference between A.I and real influencers, but for senior citizens, it is not so easy. Especially because some people cannot afford to go to the doctor for their health problems, they may rely on the internet instead. One example of fake wellness in my opinion is red light mask therapy. There isn’t really enough research backed on this topic to know whether it really does help with things such as aging. Real and A.I influencers promote this so people can buy it, but I don’t think it’s a good idea.
